content.title: About
content.content: Chicken drumsticks are the lower leg portion of the bird, consisting of meat attached to a bone. In this preparation the skin is not eaten. Drumsticks are a good source of protein, B‑vitamins, and minerals such as iron and zinc.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Drumsticks are often used in dishes that require slow braising or roasting because they stay moist.
The bones are believed to contain collagen, which may benefit joints and skin.
In many cuisines chicken drumsticks are served as a snack after marinating in soy sauce and spices.
When the skin is left on it can become crispy, but this recipe omits the skin.
Drumsticks add a rich flavor to stocks and broths.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Provides essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: Contains niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Iron and zinc contribute to immune function and hemoglobin formation.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Suitable for low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no sugar.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Collagen from the bone may help maintain joint and bone strength.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken meat.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Drumsticks contain cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can allow salmonella or campylobacter growth.

items.title: Bone hazards
items.content: The bone can pose a choking risk, especially for children.

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: If marinated in salty solutions, sodium levels can become high.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the skin‑less drumsticks by baking, boiling, braising, or grilling. After cooking, separate the meat from the bone and discard the bone. Serve with vegetables, sauces, or sliced in salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh drumsticks in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage freeze them in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Discard any that develop an off‑odor or discoloration before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken nuggets are small pieces of chicken breast that are breaded and deep‑fried or baked. They are a popular quick snack and are commonly served in fast‑food restaurants, casual eateries, and at home.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial nugget recipe was created in the 1970s by McDonald’s.
Traditional breading uses a mix of flour, breadcrumbs and spices, but there are versions with cornflakes or nut crumbs.
Nuggets are often served with sauces such as barbecue, honey‑mustard, sweet chili, cheese and others.
In some countries they are called “chicken bites” or “chicken sticks.”
Vegetarian nuggets made from soy protein mimic the taste and texture of chicken.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Nuggets contain niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken supplies iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: When prepared with a light coating, nuggets can fit into low‑carb diets.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Traditional deep‑fried nuggets are rich in saturated fat and calories, which may contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Salt in the breading and sauces increases sodium intake, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Breadings often contain gluten, dairy or egg, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Cooking at high temperatures can create trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Temperature control
items.content: Undercooked pieces may harbor harmful bacteria; ensure internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve nuggets hot, usually with dipping sauces. They can be added to salads, wraps, or used in dishes like nugget‑burgers. For a healthier option, bake at 200 °C for 15‑20 minutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked nuggets in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Frozen nuggets last up to 2 months; reheat thoroughly before eating.

egg-sandwich-on-english-muffin-with-ham.title: Egg sandwich with ham on English muffin

content.title: About
content.content: An egg sandwich with ham on an English muffin is a quick, satisfying breakfast or snack. A toasted muffin half is topped with a fried or boiled egg, a slice of ham, and often cheese, lettuce, and a sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The English muffin originated in England in the 19th century as a breakfast bread.
The egg‑and‑ham combination is a classic in American cuisine, appearing in many burgers and sandwiches.
Ham used in the sandwich can be smoked, boiled, or baked, each giving a different flavor profile.
The sandwich is easily adaptable: add avocado, swap ham for turkey, or use a whole‑grain muffin for a healthier twist.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs and ham provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin B12, while ham supplies niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Both egg and ham offer heme iron, which aids normal blood formation.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: When made with a low‑glycemic whole‑grain muffin, the sandwich fits a moderate‑carb diet.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Choosing lean ham keeps the sandwich rich in monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ham is often high in salt, so people with hypertension should limit the portion.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Egg whites can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Select ham without nitrates or excessive additives to reduce intake of potentially harmful substances.

items.title: Processed food concerns
items.content: Some ham varieties are heavily processed, which can diminish nutritional value.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Split the English muffin and toast it until golden. Cook the egg (or boil it hard‑boiled), place it on the bottom half, add a slice of ham, and optionally cheese, lettuce, and sauce. Top with the other muffin half.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The sandwich is best enjoyed fresh. If you need to store it, wrap tightly in plastic wrap and refrigerate for up to 24 hours. Muffins keep in a dry, airtight container for up to 5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Baked potato with the peel eaten is a popular side dish and standalone meal obtained by roasting whole tubers in the oven until the skin turns golden and crisp. The peel retains most of the nutrients, while baking intensifies flavor and creates a soft interior with a crunchy exterior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The potato skin contains more fiber, vitamins, and minerals than the flesh.
Baking preserves more antioxidants than boiling.
Around the world baked potatoes are served with a variety of toppings: sour cream, cheese, herbs, or spices.
Potatoes were domesticated in South America over 7,000 years ago and quickly became a staple worldwide.
Eating the skin helps lower the glycemic index of the dish.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: The skin provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and satiety.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Baked potatoes retain a significant amount of vitamin C, which aids immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance, blood pressure, and muscle function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When baked without excessive oil, the dish remains low‑calorie, suitable for weight management.

items.title: Provides vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Solanine content
items.content: If the potato has sprouted or developed green spots, the skin may contain solanine—a toxin that should be removed.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to potatoes.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Baked potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Potential contaminants
items.content: High‑temperature cooking (e.g., on foil or grill) can form acrylamide and other compounds; moderate oven temperatures are preferable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Baked potatoes with the skin can be enjoyed plain, split and topped with cheese, cottage cheese, herbs, or used in salads and sandwiches. Before baking, potatoes are often brushed with a little olive oil and seasoned with salt, pepper, and herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw tubers in a cool, dark, well‑ventilated place. After baking, let them cool, then keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the oven to restore the crisp skin.

content.title: About
content.content: Roll, multigrain is a whole‑grain roll made from a blend of wheat, rye, oats and sunflower seeds. It has a soft texture, a light nutty aroma and a mildly sweet taste. The product is suitable for breakfasts, snacks, and as a base for sandwiches.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The multigrain roll contains five main cereals, which boosts its nutritional value.
Sunflower seeds add not only flavor but also beneficial fatty acids.
The roll is baked without artificial preservatives, so it is best kept refrigerated.
Multigrain breads are often used in diet plans because they have a lower glycemic index than white bread.
Such rolls are traditionally popular in Scandinavian countries as part of a healthy breakfast.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain ingredients provide a high amount of dietary fiber, supporting normal digestion.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: The multigrain roll releases energy slowly, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B3 aid carbohydrate metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Sunflower seeds contribute a modest amount of polyunsaturated fatty acids beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The roll provides magnesium, iron and zinc, important for muscle and immune function.

items.title: Cereal allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to wheat, rye or oats.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: The product is not suitable for a gluten‑free diet.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although less calorie‑dense than white bread, it should still be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: Mold can develop during prolonged storage; always check the packaging.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roll, multigrain can be enjoyed as a snack, spread with cottage cheese, avocado or low‑fat cheese, used for sandwiches, or served alongside soups and salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the roll in a dry, cool place in an airtight package. For longer storage, keep it in the refrigerator, where it stays fresh for up to 10 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Tomatoes are the edible fruits of the tomato plant (Solanum lycopersicum), native to South America and now cultivated worldwide. They have a juicy, slightly sweet‑tart flavor and a soft yet firm texture. Tomatoes are eaten fresh and are also used to make sauces, soups, salads, and countless other dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Botanically tomatoes are classified as berries, although culinary usage treats them as vegetables.
The heaviest recorded tomato weighed over 3.5 kg.
Lycopene gives tomatoes their characteristic red color.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
There are more than 10 000 tomato varieties, differing in shape, color, and taste.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes provide a generous amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains lycopene
items.content: Lycopene is a powerful antioxidant linked to reduced risk of cardiovascular disease and certain cancers.

items.title: Supports skin health
items.content: Vitamins A and C in tomatoes help skin renewal and protect against UV‑induced damage.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in blood‑pressure regulation and proper muscle function.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Tomatoes are low in calories, making them a great choice for weight management.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The high acidity of tomatoes can aggravate gastritis or heartburn in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Improperly washed tomatoes may retain pesticide residues; thorough rinsing before consumption is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tomatoes can be eaten fresh in salads, sandwiches, and burgers, or used in sauces, soups, casseroles, and juices. Light cooking enhances lycopene absorption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store tomatoes at room temperature, away from direct sunlight, to preserve flavor and texture. For longer storage, they can be placed in the refrigerator, though this may alter taste and make the flesh firmer.

content.title: About
content.content: Tuna salad with mayonnaise is a ready‑to‑eat mixture of cooked or canned tuna combined with mayonnaise, often enriched with vegetables, herbs, and spices. It has a mild fish flavor, creamy texture, and can be served as a snack, side dish, or sandwich filling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna is one of the richest sources of omega‑3 fatty acids, beneficial for heart and brain health.
Tuna salad with mayo is popular in the United States and Japan, where it is often served as an appetizer.
Canned tuna is typically steam‑processed, preserving most of its nutrients.
Mayonnaise gives the salad a smooth texture but also adds considerable calories and fat.
The salad is frequently used in diet plans because of its high protein content.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids help reduce inflammation and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Tuna provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Supplies selenium and magnesium, which play roles in antioxidant defense and muscle function.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: The combination of protein and vitamins helps strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tuna.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned tuna often contains added salt, which can be an issue for hypertension.

items.title: Mercury
items.content: Tuna can accumulate mercury; pregnant women and children should limit consumption.

items.title: Caloric mayonnaise
items.content: Mayonnaise adds significant fat and calories, so portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tuna salad with mayo can be enjoyed on its own, spread on sandwiches, rolled in wraps, used as a filling for vegetables, or served with crackers. For extra freshness, add cucumber, onion, capers, or a squeeze of lemon juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in a sealed container. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
